notice: Original redrawn coin/artifact-inspired game devices, not historical national flags. Colors are modern readability choices. Source dates and later regional adaptations are explicit. Territory geometry and controllers are unchanged.

roman-wolf.title: British Museum 1867,0101.31, Roman didrachm, 269–266 BCE
roman-wolf.evidence: She-wolf suckling twins on Republican coinage nine or more years after our start. A deliberate near-period game adaptation, not a documented 278 BCE state flag.

croton-tripod.title: University of Colorado, Croton silver nomos, 480–430 BCE
croton-tripod.evidence: Tripod on both sides of Croton coinage, long before the campaign date.

seleucid-anchor.title: Metropolitan Museum, tetradrachm of Seleucus I, ca. 298–281 BCE
seleucid-anchor.evidence: Anchor used by Seleucus I and successors; the museum does not assert its meaning.

carthage-tanit.title: University of Ottawa, Carthaginian Tanit stele, third century BCE
carthage-tanit.evidence: Religious motif found at Carthage; not proof of an official state flag or a precise 278 BCE usage date.

ptolemy-eagle.title: Penn Museum 29-70-509, coin of Ptolemy I
ptolemy-eagle.evidence: Eagle on thunderbolt on a coin attributed to Ptolemy I.

athens-owl.title: Acropolis Museum, Athenian tetradrachm, 483–480 BCE
athens-owl.evidence: Owl and olive twig on Athenian coinage.

rhodes-rose.title: Spurlock Museum 1900.63.0010, Rhodian tetradrachm, 304–189 BCE
rhodes-rose.evidence: Rose with bud; a documented city motif in a broad dated range that includes the campaign period.

tarentum-dolphin.title: British Museum RPK,p292M.31.Tar, ca. 280–272 BCE
tarentum-dolphin.evidence: Dolphin rider on Tarentine coinage close to the campaign date.

numidian-horse.title: Santiago Padrino Fernández, Numisma 256 (2012), pp. 7–28
numidian-horse.evidence: Bearded-head/galloping-horse issues of Massinissa and successors: later than 278 BCE. Applied as regional inspiration, not either tribe’s documented 278 BCE emblem.

gallic-boar.title: Boudet and Moreau, Soulac boar standard, AFEAF 9 (1991)
gallic-boar.evidence: A real Gallic military-standard motif; proposed object date is first century BCE, later than the campaign and not attributable to individual tribes here.
